top_story: By 6 May, a fragile Iran-U.S. ceasefire was holding in name while the Strait of Hormuz became a sharper flashpoint, with alleged Iranian strikes on Fujairah and U.S. forces sinking six Iranian fast boats, exposing how quickly maritime confrontation can threaten Gulf energy infrastructure and public confidence. Later that day, Trump’s pledge that the strait would remain open if Tehran accepts a deal briefly eased market fears, driving oil prices down and stocks up, but it did not resolve the underlying military volatility. Israel’s 6 May strike on Beirut, confirmed by Netanyahu and described as the first such attack since the Lebanon ceasefire, opened a second escalatory track that widens pressure on Iran’s regional network and pushes Lebanese civilians back under the shadow of major urban bombardment. The regional picture is one of ceasefires losing deterrent value: diplomatic frameworks still shape expectations, but battlefield signaling is again setting the pace and raising the risk of broader economic and human fallout.
